clinicalPearls: An autoimmune disorder in which acquired autoantibodies neutralise factor VIII, causing sudden severe bleeding in a person with no prior bleeding history
Bleeding is typically into soft tissues, muscles, skin (extensive bruising), and mucous membranes, in contrast to the haemarthroses of congenital haemophilia
Classically presents in older adults or in the peripartum period, and is often associated with malignancy, autoimmune disease, pregnancy, or drugs, though many cases are idiopathic
The screening clue is an isolated prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time with a normal prothrombin time
A mixing study fails to correct the prolonged APTT, and correction may worsen on incubation, indicating a time- and temperature-dependent inhibitor
Diagnosis is confirmed by a low factor VIII level with a measurable factor VIII inhibitor titre
Management combines control of acute bleeding with bypassing agents and eradication of the antibody with immunosuppression
reference.pathophysiology: Acquired haemophilia A arises when the immune system generates autoantibodies against endogenous factor VIII. These inhibitors interfere with factor VIII's cofactor function in the intrinsic tenase complex, sharply reducing factor VIII activity and impairing thrombin generation. Unlike alloantibodies in congenital haemophilia, these autoantibodies often show complex, non-linear (type II) kinetics, so residual factor VIII may be detectable yet bleeding remains severe. The trigger for autoantibody formation is frequently an underlying malignancy, autoimmune condition, pregnancy, or medication, but a substantial proportion are idiopathic.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital haemophilia A with an alloantibody inhibitor
Lupus anticoagulant prolonging the APTT (typically without bleeding)
Vitamin K deficiency or liver disease affecting coagulation
additionalInvestigations: Activated partial thromboplastin time with prothrombin time to localise the defect
Mixing study, including incubated mixing, to demonstrate a time-dependent non-correcting inhibitor
Factor VIII activity assay showing a reduced level
Bethesda (or Nijmegen-modified) assay to quantify the factor VIII inhibitor titre
Von Willebrand factor studies to distinguish acquired von Willebrand syndrome
Investigation for an underlying malignancy or autoimmune disorder
redFlags: Extensive spontaneous bruising or muscle haematoma in a previously unaffected adult
Compartment syndrome or airway compromise from an expanding haematoma
Peripartum bleeding with an unexplained isolated prolonged APTT
reference.prognosis: Acute mortality is significant because of severe unheralded bleeding, but with prompt haemostatic control and antibody eradication most patients achieve remission. Relapse can occur, so monitoring after immunosuppression is important, and outcome is also influenced by any underlying disorder.
pitfalls: Attributing an isolated prolonged APTT to a lupus anticoagulant and missing a bleeding inhibitor
Omitting an incubated mixing study, so a time-dependent inhibitor is not detected
Attempting factor VIII replacement alone when a bypassing strategy is needed for high-titre inhibitors
Failing to search for an underlying malignancy or autoimmune trigger
references: Hoffman: Hematology - Basic Principles and Practice
management: Treat acute haemorrhage with bypassing agents (recombinant activated factor VII or activated prothrombin complex concentrate) or recombinant porcine factor VIII
Immunosuppressive inhibitor eradication with corticosteroids, adding rituximab or cyclophosphamide for higher-titre or refractory disease
Avoid intramuscular injections, deep venepuncture and elective invasive procedures
Screen for and manage an underlying malignancy, autoimmune disorder or peripartum trigger
Serial monitoring of factor VIII level and inhibitor titre, with prophylaxis against infection during immunosuppression
